name: Charles II of England
role: King of England, Scotland and Ireland (1660-1685)
summary: Restored to the throne in 1660 under the Declaration of Breda, he held that monarchy and the Church of England should be restored and that the crown's right came from God and descent. He sought religious indulgence for Catholics and dissenters through the 1672 Declaration, which Parliament forced him to withdraw, and he defended his brother James's succession against exclusion, dissolving Parliament several times and ruling without one from 1681.

strong-leader.rationale: Inferred: from his four dissolutions of Parliament in 1679 to 1681 and his rule without Parliament from 1681 to 1685. He stated no view on gridlock.

free-trade.rationale: No recorded position of his own; the Navigation Act 1660 was Parliament's law, to which he only assented.

revolution-justified.rationale: The 1681 declaration, as defended by Dryden, treats armed rising against a sovereign as rebellion even when feared harm is possible.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Breda claims the crown as a right that 'God and Nature hath made our due' and asks for its restoration, so he treats hereditary monarchy as legitimate.

natural-rulers.rationale: Inferred: Breda calls the crown a right that 'God and Nature hath made our due', which implies that rule by descent suits certain families by birth.

separate-church-state.rationale: He called ecclesiastical supremacy 'inherent' in the crown and kept the Church of England as the established church. Seaward reads the 1672 Indulgence as an attempt to fix the king's personal authority over the Church and religious law.

military-superiority.rationale: He took a close personal interest in naval affairs and ship design against the Dutch and French. He stated no doctrine of superiority.

restore-past-order.rationale: Breda seeks the restoration of king, peers and people to their 'just, ancient and fundamental rights'. He did not weigh order against progress.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Breda promises to be advised by a free Parliament and to consent to Acts of Parliament, but it also grounds the crown in God and Nature. The evidence points both ways.

separated-powers.rationale: Wikipedia records that he replaced judges and sheriffs at will and packed juries against Whigs in the 1680s. He stated no view on the separation of powers.

head-commands-forces.rationale: He dismissed Clarendon, chose the Cabal and later Danby as ministers, and ran the Irish Squadron directly. The Commons impeached Danby, but he stated no doctrine on this.

church-by-bishops.rationale: The 1672 declaration preserves the 'doctrine, discipline, and government' of the Church of England as established by law. It does not name bishops.

death-penalty.rationale: Nine regicides were executed after the Act of Indemnity and Oblivion excluded them from pardon. He stated no general view on capital punishment.

religious-exemptions.rationale: The 1672 declaration suspended the penal laws for nonconformists and let Catholics worship in private houses. He withdrew it in 1673 after Parliament objected.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The 1672 declaration asserts the crown's supreme power in ecclesiastical matters, yet it keeps tithes, revenues and benefices for the established clergy. The evidence is mixed.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: He sided openly with the Tories against the Exclusion Bill in 1679 to 1681, so he did not stand above party. He stated no principle on this.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The 1672 declaration claimed a power to suspend penal statutes 'inherent in us', but he withdrew it in 1673 when Parliament objected, so the position is mixed.

elective-rulers.rationale: Breda grounds the crown in descent and God's gift, not election, and the 1681 declaration says the succession will be 'preserved in its due descent'.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The 1681 declaration, as defended by Dryden, says a subject may not rise in arms against a sovereign, even one of another religion, and calls that rebellion.

parliament-supreme.rationale: He personally dissolved Parliament four times in 1679 to 1681 and ruled without one from 1681 to 1685. In 1672 he claimed a supreme power 'inherent in us' over penal laws, though he withdrew that declaration in 1673.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Inferred: the 1670 Dover pension was meant to make him financially independent of Parliament, a motive historians debate. The treaty's aim is documented, but the wider view is not stated.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Wikipedia records prosecutions, seized estates, a forfeited London charter and disenfranchised Whigs in 1681 to 1683. He stated no principle for this.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: No recorded position of his own; the Navigation Act 1660 was Parliament's law, to which he only assented.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Breda gives his title 'by the Grace of God' and calls the crown a right that God and Nature made due. It does not speak to the people's role in authority.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The 1681 declaration, as quoted by Dryden, insists on the succession being preserved in its due descent, and he backed his brother James against exclusion. The statement names a child, which he did not address.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: He began the Third Anglo-Dutch War in 1672. The Treaty of Dover committed him to back a French invasion of the Dutch Republic, and the Second Dutch War began with English attempts on Dutch possessions.

national-church-status.rationale: The 1672 declaration says the Church of England shall 'be preserved and remain entire' as established by law and that only exactly conformable clergy may hold benefices.

notes: Assent to the Clarendon Code (Conventicle, Five Mile and Uniformity Acts), the Test Act and the 1662 Licensing Act is not counted, as these were Parliament's laws he assented to. The Navigation Acts are treated the same way, and only the 1660 act's effects are used. The Secret Treaty of Dover's Catholic conversion clause is documented only through secondary reporting, and the Dover pension is cited as a motive historians debate. Wikisource copies of the 1672 Declaration and the Dover treaty were not reachable; the 1672 text used is from constitution.org. The king's 1681 Oxford declaration was not found in full; its content is taken from Dryden's quotations in His Majesties Declaration Defended. The Royal Society charters (1662 and 1663) are noted as royal patronage but support no statement. His deathbed reception into the Catholic Church is noted in Wikipedia as uncertain in conscious commitment, so it is not used to answer any statement.
